**I pick candidate 6.** I worked this out in my head from rough totals and costs, not a full day-by-day simulation, so treat the margins below as estimates.

1. **How often to order.** A day with any order costs 45, and the average stock to pay holding on is about half of what one order brings in. Daily demand is about 12 of product 0 and 38 of product 1, so each extra day between orders adds about 25 units of average stock, or about 15 per day in holding.
   - **Daily orders (candidate 3):** 26 order days cost about 1170, which is about 585 more than ordering every 2 days. They save only about 450 in holding, so they come out about 135 worse.
   - **Every 3 days (candidates 0 and 1):** 9 orders instead of 13 save 180. They add about 450 in holding over 30 days, so they come out about 270 worse.
   - **Capacity risk:** at 3–4 day cycles, a product 1 delivery of 130–175 units lands on top of leftover stock. Product 0 arrives the next day, so the 200-unit limit can be exceeded and the excess is lost. Candidate 4 (every 4 days, deliveries of about 167) is the most exposed.
   - So ordering every 2 days is best. That leaves candidates 2, 5, 6 and 7.

2. **How much to order (product 1 decides it).**
   - Forecast demand for 30 days is 1165. With the average multiplier of about 1.046, expected demand is about 1219.
   - Before the first delivery on day 4, forecast demand for days 0–3 is 125 against 51 in stock. About 74 units go unmet no matter which plan you choose.
   - Total supply, including the starting 51:
     - **Candidate 2:** about 1328, roughly 180 more than can be sold. That surplus ends up written off or left at the end, costing about 11–14 per unit.
     - **Candidate 6:** about 1196, roughly 70 above sellable demand. That is a reasonable cushion.
     - **Candidates 5 and 7:** about 1155 and less. They will run short more often, at a cost of about 13 per missing unit (lost margin 6 plus penalty 7).
   - A shortage costs about 13 per unit and a surplus about 14, so the best target is roughly the expected demand with a moderate cushion. Candidate 6 is closest to that. Its small buffer also makes it the most robust if actual demand moves away from the forecast.

**My choice is candidate 6.** It is the best estimate, but only with moderate confidence. Everything below was worked out in my head on forecast averages. I did not simulate anything.

**How I compared them:**
- **Order size against expected demand.** For each plan, I compared the order with the forecast demand (×1.046) for the days that delivery has to cover. Product 0 arrives 5 days after ordering and product 1 after 4, so I checked each product against its own window.
- **Cost of an order day.** Each day with an order costs 45. Ordering less often means fewer of those fees but more stock sitting on the shelf.

**Where the other plans lose:**
- **Candidate 4** orders every 4 days, about 215 units at a time. That doesn't fit in the 200-unit warehouse once leftover stock is counted, so part of each delivery is lost.
- **Candidate 3** orders every day, which is 26 order days at 45 each. That is about 585 more than a plan ordering every other day. Daily orders do keep stock lower, but that saves only about 355 in storage, so it still comes out roughly 230 behind.
- **Candidates 0 and 1** order every 3 days. They save about 180 in order fees compared with every other day. But they hold more stock on average (about one day's demand instead of half a day's), which costs about 355 more in storage. On average they lose about 175. They also come close to the 200-unit limit, especially around the demand spike on day 19.
- **Candidate 2** orders every other day but about 20% above expected demand. The plan is fixed and doesn't react to actual sales, so the surplus builds up. That adds storage costs, risks overflowing the warehouse, and leads to write-offs when stock expires.
- **Candidate 7** orders about 4% below expected demand. A shortage costs about 13 per unit (lost margin plus the penalty), while a spare unit costs only about 1 to store. Ordering below demand is the wrong direction.
- **Candidate 5** matches expected demand almost exactly, with no buffer. Because nothing adjusts to actual sales, random misses add up, and shortages are expensive.

**Why candidate 6 wins:** It orders every other day with a buffer of about 5% above expected demand. That is enough to cover random swings without piling up stock that ends up in storage or written off. It is also the most robust to demand differing from the forecast.

Shortages on days 0–4 can't be avoided in any plan, because the opening stock is too small and the first orders don't arrive until days 4–5.

My pick is **candidate 6**. I worked through the rules by hand and used no tools. My confidence is moderate, mainly in the choice between candidates 6 and 5.

1. **Start of the month.** Nothing ordered arrives before day 4 (product 1) or day 5 (product 0). The early shortages are therefore the same for every plan and don't separate them.

2. **Ordering costs.** Each ordering day costs 45.
   - Candidate 3 orders on 26 days, so it pays 1170.
   - Candidates 2, 5, 6 and 7 order every 2 days (13 days), so they pay 585.
   - Candidates 0 and 1 order every 3 days (9 days), so they pay 405.
   - Candidate 4 orders every 4 days (7 days), so it pays 315.

3. **Storage costs and warehouse space.** The longer the gap between orders, the more stock sits in the warehouse each evening.
   - A 3-day cycle holds about half a day's demand more than a 2-day cycle. That costs about 14 per day, or roughly 340 over the month, which outweighs the 180 saved on ordering days.
   - Candidate 0 also overfills the 200-unit warehouse. Following it on the forecast, 11 units are lost on day 10 and 21 on day 13.
   - Candidate 4 is worse. Its product-1 deliveries alone are 152–170 units, plus whatever is already in stock, so it regularly loses stock to the cap.
   - Daily ordering (candidate 3) saves about 340 on storage but pays about 585 more in ordering costs than the 2-day plans.

4. **Order size among the 2-day plans.** Measured against the forecast demand each delivery has to cover, the plans order:
   - candidate 7: about 1.0× the forecast;
   - candidate 5: about 1.05×;
   - candidate 6: about 1.1×;
   - candidate 2: about 1.25×.

   Actual demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast on average. A missing unit costs much more than a spare one. For product 1 that is 13 (lost margin 6 plus penalty 7) against 0.5 per day of storage. Spare stock also carries over, since goods keep for 9 days. So ordering slightly above the forecast pays off.
   - Candidate 7 will often run short.
   - Candidate 2 over-orders by about 20% every cycle. The surplus builds up, raises storage costs, and risks spoiling.
   - Candidate 6 gives a reasonable safety margin, including for the day-19 spike (95 units of product 1).

Candidate 6 is clearly ahead of the 3-day, 4-day and daily plans. Its lead over candidate 5 comes only from my estimate of the safety margin, which is why my confidence is only moderate.

I picked **candidate 6**. I estimated this in my head, not by simulation, so it's a judgement and not an exact count.

1. **Order frequency.** Ordering every 2 days is the best balance.
   - Daily ordering (candidate 3) pays the 45 fee 25 times instead of 13, which costs about 540 more.
   - With orders every 3 days, you pay the fee 4 fewer times and save about 180. But you carry about half a day's demand more stock each evening. That costs about 0.5 × 38 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 11 × 0.7 ≈ 13.5 a day, or about 350 over 26 days.
   - Ordering every 4 days (candidate 4) brings about 215 units per delivery, which risks hitting the 200-unit limit, and the excess is lost.
2. **Order size among the every-2-days plans.**
   - Goods keep for 9 days, so leftovers simply carry into the next cycle. What really matters is the total ordered against expected demand. For product 1 over days 4–29, that is 1040 × 1.046 ≈ 1088.
   - Candidate 2 orders 1277 units. About 190 of them would be left over and wasted at 11 each.
   - Candidate 7 orders 1040, below the expected 1088, so it would run short often. Each unit short costs about 13 (lost margin 6 + penalty 7).
   - Candidate 5 orders 1104, which leaves almost no buffer.
   - Candidate 6 orders 1145, a buffer of about 57 units. That is about one standard deviation of total demand, which fits since a unit short (≈13) costs slightly more than a unit wasted (11).
   - For product 0, candidate 6 orders 305 against expected demand of about 290, which is also reasonable.

I estimate **candidate 6** gives the highest expected profit. I worked this out by reasoning only; I didn't run a simulation.

1. **Order frequency.**
   - **Every 4 days (candidate 4):** each delivery is about 200 units on top of what's still in stock. Anything over the 200-unit capacity is lost, and it's already been paid for.
   - **Every 3 days (candidates 0 and 1):** deliveries are about 170 units, so on days with high leftover stock they're close to the limit.
   - **Every day (candidate 3):** this pays the 45 fee about 26 times instead of 13, roughly 585 extra.
   - **Every 2 days (candidates 2, 5, 6, 7):** this is the best trade-off.

2. **How much is needed.** Opening stock (24 and 51 units) runs out within the first few days, before the first orders arrive. Orders then have to cover expected demand of about 290 units of item 0 (days 5–29) and about 1088 units of item 1 (days 4–29). These figures include the average multiplier of about 1.046.

3. **Order totals of the every-2-days plans for item 1:**

   | Plan | Total ordered | Versus ≈1088 needed |
   |---|---|---|
   | 2 | ≈1277 | about 190 units left over at the end (≈2000 in purchase cost) |
   | 6 | ≈1145 | about 5% above demand |
   | 5 | ≈1104 | about equal to demand |
   | 7 | ≈1040 | below demand |

   Running out costs 13 per unit (6 in lost margin plus a penalty of 7). A surplus unit costs little mid-period, because it keeps for 9 days and sells at the next shortage. It only becomes a full loss at the end of the horizon. So a small margin above demand is worth it.

4. **Item 0 in candidate 6.** It orders 305 units against about 290 expected, which is also a reasonable margin.

Candidate 6 has the right order frequency and a moderate safety margin without large leftovers at the end.

I pick **candidate 6**. It is the only plan that combines every-other-day ordering, totals close to expected demand, and no lost space at the 200-unit warehouse limit. These are mental estimates on forecast values; nothing was simulated.

**1. All plans start the same way.** Opening stock (24 units of product 0, 51 of product 1) runs out before the first deliveries. Over days 0–3, product 1 demand is 125. Over days 0–4, product 0 demand is 68. So every candidate pays roughly the same shortage penalties at the start.

**2. Ordering every four days loses stock (candidate 4).** Batches of about 48 + 167 = 215 units, plus leftover stock, exceed the 200-unit limit. The surplus is lost on arrival even though it was paid for.

**3. Ordering every three days (candidates 0, 1) costs more in storage.** Product 1 batches are about 120–136, so far more sits on the shelf each evening than with every-other-day ordering. Fewer orders save about 180 in order fees. The extra storage costs more than that, and with leftovers the 200-unit limit is close.

**4. Daily ordering (candidate 3) costs more in fees.** It places 26 orders at 45 each, or 1,170. The every-other-day plans place 13 orders, saving about 585. Storage in those plans is higher by about half a day's demand: about 9.5 per day for product 1 and 4.2 for product 0, so about 360 over the period. That leaves the every-other-day plans ahead by about 225.

**5. Among the every-other-day plans (2, 5, 6, 7), the deciding factor is how much they order.** Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.

| | Product 1 | Product 0 |
|---|---|---|
| Expected demand, forecast × 1.046 | about 1,088 (days 4–29) | about 290 (days 5–29) |
| Candidate 2 | 1,277 | — |
| Candidate 6 | 1,145 | 325 |
| Candidate 5 | 1,104 | 295 |
| Candidate 7 | 1,040 | — |

- Candidate 2 orders about 17% above expected demand, so it carries extra storage cost and wastes stock at the end.
- Candidate 7 orders below expected demand, so it runs short.
- Candidates 5 and 6 are close. A shortage costs more than a leftover: for product 1, 13 lost per unit short versus 11 plus storage per unit left over, and for product 0, 10 versus 0.7 per day.
- Mid-period surplus carries over because goods keep for 9 days, so it only costs storage. That makes 6's modest margin (about 5% for product 1) the safer choice when demand varies, which is about ±30% per day.

I chose **candidate 6**: a delivery every two days, ordering a little more than average demand. This is an estimate worked out by hand from rounded per-day costs, not a full simulation. Candidates 5 and 6 are close.

1. **How often to order.** I compared the €45 order fee against holding costs, counting the average stock left at the end of each day.
   - Every day (candidate 3): about 45 per day, almost all of it order fees.
   - Every two days (candidates 2, 5, 6, 7): about 22.5 + 13.4 ≈ 36 per day.
   - Every three days (candidates 0, 1): about 15 + 26.7 ≈ 42 per day.
   - Every four days (candidate 4): the most expensive of the three batch options.

   So the two-day schedule is cheapest. Over about 25 days, three-day batches save about 180 in order fees but cost about 330 more in holding.

2. **How much to order in total.** The plan is fixed in advance, so over-ordering builds up and spoils, and under-ordering loses sales.
   - Expected demand for product 1, days 4–29, is about 1,040 × 1.046 ≈ 1,088 (days 0–3 are covered by the starting stock).
   - Totals ordered: candidate 2 orders 1,277 (too much), 5 orders 1,104, 6 orders 1,145 and 7 orders 1,040 (too little).
   - Running short costs 13 per unit (6 lost margin + 7 penalty). Leftover stock costs 11 per unit plus holding. Shortfalls on one day aren't recovered later, while surplus carries forward, so ordering slightly above average pays off. That favours candidate 6, with candidate 5 close behind.
   - For product 0, expected demand is about 290. Candidate 6 orders 305 and candidate 5 orders 295; both are reasonable. Candidate 2 orders 349, which is too much.

3. **Warehouse capacity.** Two-day batches never come close to the 200-unit limit, so nothing is lost when deliveries arrive.

I pick **candidate 6**: it orders every second day with a moderate safety buffer. Candidate 5 is a close second. I worked this out roughly in my head, not with a step-by-step simulation.

**What every plan loses.** No delivery can arrive before day 4 for product 1 or day 5 for product 0. So all plans run short at the start: about 74 units of product 1 and 44 of product 0, roughly 780 in penalties. This doesn't separate the candidates.

**Candidate 4 (orders every 4 days).** Each delivery is about 215 units, above the 200-unit capacity. The surplus is lost on arrival, already paid for. This is the weakest plan.

**Candidates 0 and 1 (every 3 days).** They make about 4 fewer orders than the every-2-day plans, saving about 180 in order fees. But they carry roughly 25 more units of stock, which costs about 340 in storage over the month. They also risk overflowing the 200 limit when a delivery lands on top of leftover stock. Candidate 0 also orders about 1214 units of product 1, which is too many.

**Candidate 3 (orders daily).** It pays the 45 order fee about 26 times. That is roughly 560 more than ordering every 2 days, and the lower storage cost doesn't make up for it.

**Every-2-day plans (2, 5, 6, 7).** These differ in how much they order. Expected product 1 demand for days 4–29 is about 1040 at forecast, or about 1088 once you include the 1.046 average multiplier. Total ordered:
- **Candidate 2:** 1277, about 190 surplus. That is roughly 2000 of stock left over at the end, plus a risk of overflow around the day-19 demand spike.
- **Candidate 7:** 1040, exactly the forecast. With the multiplier it falls short on average, so it pays penalties.
- **Candidate 5:** 1104, almost no buffer. Because lost sales aren't recovered, stock drifts down to zero and it runs short repeatedly, around 50 units over the month.
- **Candidate 6:** 1145, about 57 above expected demand, or about 4–5 units per cycle. A unit short costs 13 (6 lost margin plus 7 penalty). An extra unit costs about 11 plus storage, and only if it's still unsold at the end. Under random demand that trade-off favours a moderate buffer, and candidate 6 has one.

I'd pick **candidate 6**, with moderate confidence. I worked this out in my head, so the figures are rough.

**Losses every plan shares.** Nothing ordered can arrive before day 4 for product 1 or day 5 for product 0. On the forecast, days 0–3 run about 74 units of product 1 short, and days 0–4 about 44 units of product 0 short. Every plan pays these penalties.

**Order frequency:**
- **Every 4 days (candidate 4):** each delivery of product 1 is about 152–170 units. Add the product 0 still in stock and the leftovers, and the 200-unit warehouse overflows almost every time. Units that overflow are paid for and lost, so this plan is the weakest.
- **Every 3 days (candidates 0, 1):** these pay the 45 fee 9 times, which is 405. Each delivery holds more stock, so storage costs roughly 330 more than ordering every 2 days. The 175 units of product 1 that arrive on day 19 likely overflow by about 10–15 units. Candidate 0 also orders too much overall: about 1214 units of product 1 against roughly 1088 expected demand.
- **Every day (candidate 3):** 26 order fees come to 1170. That is 585 more than ordering every 2 days, and the storage savings don't make up for it.
- **Every 2 days (candidates 2, 5, 6, 7):** 13 fees come to 585. Deliveries are smaller, so the warehouse limit is hardly an issue. This is the best balance of fees against storage costs.

**Choosing among the every-2-day plans.** The deciding factor is the total product 1 ordered for days 4–29. Demand totals 1040 on the forecast, or about 1088 once you apply the 1.046 average multiplier.
- **Candidate 7:** orders 1040, exactly the forecast. It ignores the 1.046 multiplier, so there will be regular shortfalls at 13 per unit (6 lost margin plus the 7 penalty).
- **Candidate 5:** orders 1104, only about 16 above expected demand. That buffer is too thin.
- **Candidate 2:** orders 1277, about 190 too many. Each unsold unit costs 11, and the 165 units arriving on day 18 overflow the warehouse.
- **Candidate 6:** orders 1145, about 57 above expected demand, which is roughly one standard deviation of total demand. Unsold stock carries over to later days, so a shortage (13) costs more than holding extra (about 0.5 per day). That supports this moderate buffer. For product 0 it orders 305 against about 290 expected.

It's closest between candidate 6 and candidate 1. Candidate 1 saves 180 on order fees but probably pays more for storage and overflow.

I chose **candidate 2**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation of the plans.

1. **Daily ordering (candidate 3)** costs too much in fixed fees: 26 order days × 45 = 1170.
2. **Ordering every 4 days (candidate 4)** brings about 215 units per delivery. With leftover stock, that can go over the 200-unit capacity, and the excess is lost after being paid for.
3. **Every 3 days vs. every 2 days.** Ordering every 3 days (candidates 0 and 1) means 9 order days instead of 13, which saves about 180 in fixed fees. But stock sits on the shelf longer. Holding stock about one extra day costs roughly 9.5 a day for product 1 and 3.9 a day for product 0. Over about 25 days that adds roughly 350. So ordering every 2 days comes out ahead overall, and it also carries less risk of going over capacity.
4. **Among the every-2-days plans (2, 5, 6, 7)**, the bigger orders are better:
   - A unit of shortage costs a lot: for product 1, the lost margin of 6 plus the penalty of 7 makes 13.
   - Ordering too much costs little. Shelf life is 9 days, so leftovers simply carry over to the next cycle, at a holding cost of only about 1 per unit.
   - Candidate 2 orders about 20% above the expected 2-day demand (for example, 89 units against an expected ~74). Candidates 5, 6 and 7 order only about 5% above expected demand or less.

I pick **Candidate 6**, with moderate confidence. I worked from approximate mental estimates, not a full step-by-step simulation, so the cost figures below are rough.

**What all plans share.** The first deliveries arrive on day 4 (product 1) and day 5 (product 0). Starting stock can't cover demand before then, so every candidate takes roughly the same early shortage: about 74 units of product 1 and 44 of product 0.

**What separates the plans.**
- **Order size against demand.** A missing unit of product 1 costs 13 (6 lost margin plus a 7 penalty). An extra unit only costs storage until the next delivery, because shelf life is 9 days and leftovers carry over. So a small surplus over forecast pays off. Actual demand averages about 1.046× forecast, so a plan has a real buffer only if it orders above that.
  - Candidate 2 orders about 1.25× forecast demand for each cycle. That builds 16–20 surplus units of product 1 every cycle, which leads to spoilage, high storage costs and overflow.
  - Candidates 5 and 7 order about 1.0–1.06×, which is at or below average actual demand. That leaves no buffer, so they will run short.
  - Candidate 6 orders about 1.1×. That leaves a moderate buffer that grows slowly.
- **How often to order.** Each order day costs 45.
  - Candidate 3 orders every day (26 order days, 1,170). It keeps stock low, but compared with ordering every other day it saves only about 360 in storage while paying about 585 more in order fees.
  - Candidates 0 and 1 order every 3 days (9 order days), and Candidate 4 every 4 days (7 order days). They save on order fees, but each delivery is 150–215 units. With leftovers, stock on arrival gets close to the 200-unit limit or goes over it, and the excess is lost after it has already been paid for. They also carry about 25 more units of stock on average, which is roughly 360 more in storage. With random demand, the risk of overflow followed by shortages before the next delivery is highest for these plans.
- **Ordering every other day** (13 order days, 585) is the best balance. Among those plans, Candidate 6 has the right order size: enough buffer to avoid most shortages without piling up stock that spoils.

1. **How often to order.** Every order day costs a fixed 45, but bigger, less frequent orders mean more stock sitting in the warehouse and paying storage.
   - **Every 2 days (candidates 2, 5, 6, 7):** about 12 order days, roughly 540 in fees.
   - **Every 3 days (candidates 0, 1):** saves about 135 in fees. But each batch is about half as large again as a 2-day batch. That adds about 25 units of average stock and roughly 400 in storage. Batches of about 130 of product 1 can also hit the 200-unit warehouse limit.
   - **Every 4 days (candidate 4):** the same problem, only worse.
   - **Daily (candidate 3):** about 13 extra order days, around 585 more in fees. That is more than the roughly 400 it saves on storage.

   Ordering every 2 days comes out best.

2. **How much to order among the 2-day plans.** Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. One missing unit of product 1 costs 13 (6 of lost margin plus the 7 penalty). One extra unit costs only 0.5 per day in storage, because leftovers carry over to later days. So ordering a little above expected demand pays off.
   - **Candidate 7** orders about 1.00 × forecast. That is below expected demand, so it will run short often.
   - **Candidate 5** orders about 1.06 × forecast, close to expected demand, which leaves almost no buffer.
   - **Candidate 6** orders about 1.10 × forecast. The surplus builds up by only about 2 units of product 1 per day, which costs roughly 300 in storage and cuts down on shortages.

Я выбираю **кандидата 6**. Всё посчитано в уме и приближённо, поэтому расклад ниже — грубая оценка, а не точный результат.

**Частота заказа.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 45, а запас между поставками стоит денег за хранение. В среднем спрос около 52 единиц в день, хранение примерно 0,55 за единицу в день. Если заказывать раз в k дней, среднее вечернее хранение обходится примерно в 14,3·(k−1) в день, то есть около 370·(k−1) за период.

| Как часто заказывают | Кандидаты | Плата за заказы | Хранение | Итого |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Каждый день | 3 | ≈1170 | ≈0 | ≈1170 |
| Раз в 2 дня | 2, 5, 6, 7 | ≈585 | ≈370 | **≈955** |
| Раз в 3 дня | 0, 1 | ≈405 | ≈740 | ≈1150 |
| Раз в 4 дня | 4 | ≈315 | ≈1100 | ≈1430 |

У кандидата 4 есть ещё одна проблема: на 8–9 день на складе около 180–190 единиц при вместимости 200. При спросе ниже прогноза излишек при приходе пропадёт. У кандидата 0 похожий риск, потому что он заказывает с запасом около 1,2.

**Запас сверх прогноза у планов «раз в 2 дня».** Я поделил каждый заказ на прогноз спроса за дни, которые он покрывает:
- **Кандидат 7 — около 1,0.** Это ниже среднего множителя спроса 1,046, поэтому нехватка будет копиться. Каждая непроданная единица стоит упущенной маржи плюс неустойки, то есть 13 для товара 1.
- **Кандидат 5 — около 1,05.** Запас почти равен среднему спросу, на случайные всплески его не хватит.
- **Кандидат 6 — около 1,10.** Небольшой запас на случай отклонений, излишек не уходит в списание.
- **Кандидат 2 — около 1,25.** Излишек растёт примерно на 10 единиц в день. Он уходит в хранение и списание по сроку годности. Кроме того, на 18 день есть риск переполнить склад: придёт 165 единиц товара 1 плюс остатки.

**Устойчивость.** Нехватка обходится примерно в 13 за единицу, а лишняя единица — всего около 0,5 за день хранения. Поэтому запас около 10 % — разумный компромисс, если спрос отклонится от прогноза. Даже в пиковые дни 18–19 запас у кандидата 6 около 1,10, и склад не переполняется.

I picked **candidate 2**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation, so treat it as a reasoned choice rather than a verified optimum.

1. **How often to order.** Combined demand is about 50 units a day. Each order day costs 45, and holding costs about 0.5–0.7 per unit per day. The usual ordering-versus-holding trade-off (the economic order quantity) gives a batch of about √(2·45·50/0.55) ≈ 90 units, which is roughly one order every 2 days.
   - Ordering daily (candidate 3) costs about 585 more in ordering fees, but saves only about 400 in holding.
   - Ordering every 3–4 days (candidates 0, 1, 4) holds a lot more stock. It also risks hitting the 200-unit warehouse limit, especially around the order of about 175 units of product 1 for the demand spike on day 19.

2. **Which 2-day plan.** That leaves candidates 2, 5, 6 and 7. A missing unit of product 1 costs 13 (6 lost margin plus a 7 penalty). An extra unit just carries to the next cycle at about 0.5 per day, because shelf life is 9 days. So it pays to keep a generous safety stock. Candidate 2 orders about 90 units of product 1 per 2-day cycle against average demand of about 75, the largest buffer of the four. It also ends with a moderate last order (day 24: 11 and 90 units), so not much goes to waste at the end.

I chose **candidate 2**. This is an estimate worked out in my head from the forecast means, without running a simulation.

**How often to order.** Each order day costs 45, and holding stock costs roughly 0.55 per unit per day.
- **Every 3 days (candidates 0 and 1):** 9 order days cost 405. Average stock is about 25 units higher than with a 2-day cycle, which adds roughly 400 in holding. That outweighs the 180 saved on order fees.
- **Every 4 days (candidate 4):** each delivery round is about 215 units, so with leftover stock it runs into the 200-unit capacity. The excess is lost but already paid for.
- **Every day (candidate 3):** 30 order days cost 1350, which is about 765 more than ordering every 2 days. Lower stock saves only about 400 in holding.
- **Every 2 days (candidates 2, 5, 6, 7):** this is the best trade-off.

**Choosing among the 2-day plans.** I compared total supply (start stock plus everything delivered by day 29) with expected demand. Expected demand is the forecast total × 1.046.
- **Product 1:** expected demand is about 1219.
  - Candidate 2 supplies about 1328, a surplus of about 109.
  - Candidate 6 supplies about 1196, slightly short.
  - Candidate 5 supplies about 1155, short.
  - Candidate 7 supplies less still.
- **Product 0:** expected demand is about 361. Candidate 2 supplies about 373. Candidate 6 supplies about 349.

**Why a surplus pays off.** A missing unit of product 1 costs 13 (lost margin of 6 plus the penalty of 7). An extra unit that never sells costs 11 plus some holding. So an extra unit is worth buying if it has better than about a 46% chance of being sold.
